title: Turkey brightens the outlook for peace
text:
Turkey brightens the outlook for peace
Loading...
In a region that’s a flash point for unrest, Turkey has taken a key step toward calming domestic as well as cross-border tensions – and it's one that could lead to new conceptions of national identity that transcend ethnic or linguistic differences.
On Monday, the country’s parliament overwhelmingly voted for a landmark bill aimed at conclusively ending more than 40 years of conflict with its substantial Kurdish ethnic minority. The legislation outlines processes for conditional amnesties and the reintegration of thousands of Kurds, including armed combatants who have lived or operated from strongholds in neighboring Iran, Iraq, and Syria for decades. (An estimated 31 million Kurds are spread across all four countries, and various factions have fought for independence or greater autonomy.)
Turkey’s separatist Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) – designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States, and the European Union – abandoned the goal of full independence a few decades ago. And in May 2025, it announced it would disband and disarm, thus putting the onus on the Turkish government to move the process along.
“Many Kurds cautiously welcome the move as a chance to pivot toward democratic struggle,” Garo Paylan, a visiting scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said at the time. But, he noted, they would want to see “concrete commitments on political representation, cultural rights, and the reintegration of Kurdish voices into public life.”
Last week, long-imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan described the pending legislation as “the beginning of a democratisation process that will be at least as significant as the founding of the Republic,” which was established in 1920 after the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire.
This phase of reconciliation positions Turkey – a key and well-armed member of NATO – to exert a constructive and stabilizing influence in the region. Ankara had been at loggerheads with Syria for several years, believing it was aiding large numbers of PKK fighters. It also regularly conducted military raids and held territory in Iraq’s Kurdistan region. But last year, within three months of the PKK announcement, Turkish attacks on Iraqi territory fell by 97%, according to an international rights organization. Now, Turkey is helping Iraq and other oil-producing Gulf States export and import goods across Turkish roadways, while the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked. Similarly, it could also support Syria’s recovery from civil war.
The key challenge is at home – as well as in the EU, which Turkey has long sought to join – as Turkish citizens await tangible evidence of a more inclusive and responsive political system. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has been consolidating power and silencing dissent in recent years. Several opposition skeptics view his gestures of peace toward Kurds as little more than a political ploy to gain popularity and extend his term in office.
But Zakir Avşar, a professor at Ankara’s Hacı Bayram Veli University, urges a more magnanimous view of developments. What’s important, he told the local Daily Sabah newspaper on Tuesday, is attaining a balance among “security and freedom, public order and democratic politics, ... and citizens’ sense of belonging.”
“The success of this process,” in Mr. Avşar’s words, “should ... be measured not by the political advantage it provides to one side over another, but by its contribution to Türkiye’s common future.”
